description: I am a data scientist interested in satellite data, GIS, AI, and geospatial analytics. I use Earth observation and open data to explore real-world challenges such as agriculture, environmental change, and disaster monitoring.
summary:
RiceShift is a decision-support prototype for California rice farms developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data” challenge.

Its goal is to help determine when continuous rice production should remain the preferred option and when a winter rotation—such as vetch or a cover-crop mixture—deserves consideration.

RiceShift combines NASA MODIS and SMAP Earth observations with USDA crop-history data, NASS agricultural statistics, NRCS SSURGO soil properties, and published UC Davis / UC ANR agronomic research. The workflow first identifies long-term rice areas, then tests whether winter represents a distinct environmental management window, evaluates whether NASA indicators provide useful agricultural signals, screens soil feasibility, and finally adds published evidence on nitrogen contribution, rice response, cover-crop performance, and economic context.

The results show that NASA observations can provide valuable environmental evidence, but should not select a crop by themselves. RiceShift therefore uses NASA data to identify environmental opportunity, then combines crop history, soil constraints, agronomy, economics, and farmer objectives to support a practical rotation decision.

This approach is important because successful rotation is not simply about growing more crops—it is about improving whole-farm value and resilience without creating unacceptable agronomic or economic risk.
details:
RiceShift is a reproducible decision-support prototype that explores when California rice farms should continue with rice and when a winter rotation, such as vetch or a cover-crop mixture, may deserve consideration.

A central design principle of this project was to avoid turning the technical method itself into the objective. Modern AI-assisted development makes it possible to generate code quickly, but selecting the right question, data, assumptions, and validation methods still requires scientific judgment. I therefore began with the agricultural decision that needed to be supported and worked backward to determine what evidence would actually be useful.

My background includes geophysics, satellite-data analysis, GIS, data science, and software engineering. For RiceShift, I also reviewed agricultural and soil-science literature and incorporated published research from UC Davis and UC Agriculture and Natural Resources. Agriculture is a multidisciplinary problem involving climate, water, soil, remote sensing, agronomy, economics, and land management. I designed RiceShift around the idea that no single dataset or model should be expected to answer the entire question.

The prototype combines NASA MODIS and SMAP Earth observations with USDA Cropland Data Layer data, NASS agricultural statistics, NRCS SSURGO soil properties, county agricultural reports, and published California field experiments. The analysis first establishes long-term rice-production areas, then tests seasonal environmental differences, evaluates NASA indicators against agricultural outcomes, screens soil feasibility, and finally adds agronomic and economic evidence for winter rotation.

An important result was also a limitation: NASA observations alone were not strong enough to serve as a stand-alone yield or crop-selection model. Instead of forcing a more complex machine-learning model to produce a stronger-looking result, RiceShift uses NASA data where they are most defensible—as an environmental evidence layer—and combines them with soil, crop history, agronomic research, and farm objectives.

I implemented the project in Python using pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, Rasterio, GeoPandas, Matplotlib, and related geospatial tools. The final demonstration is delivered as a Jupyter Notebook running in Google Colaboratory so that both the executable code and the scientific reasoning can be reviewed together. The notebook can be reproduced directly from the public GitHub repository.

AI tools, including Gemini available in Google Colaboratory, were used as development assistants for coding, debugging, and implementation support. However, the project objectives, data selection, literature interpretation, hypotheses, statistical tests, validation strategy, and conclusions were deliberately selected and reviewed to keep the analysis focused on the agricultural decision rather than on the technology itself.

The intended impact of RiceShift is not to automatically tell a farmer which crop to plant. It is to demonstrate a transparent framework for combining Earth observations with local agricultural evidence so that crop-rotation decisions can be made with better environmental, agronomic, and economic context.
